sections.figure_alt: A weight whose magnitude rises with frequency.
sections.body_md:
A nominal plant \(P_0\) is a model, not the hardware. Uncertainty is the explicit statement of how far the hardware may be from that model. Two shapes cover most of the statements used in loop design. An additive weight bounds the absolute error \(|P - P_0|\). A multiplicative weight bounds the relative error \(|P - P_0|/|P_0|\).

A parameter that simply sits in an interval, such as a gain known to ten percent, is parametric uncertainty. A resonance that was never written into \(P_0\) is dynamic uncertainty. Dynamic error is usually small at low frequency, where the model was fitted, and large at high frequency, where the neglected modes live. The weight is drawn so that it grows there.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
Additive form: \(P = P_0 + W_a \Delta\) with \(|\Delta| \le 1\), so \(|P - P_0| \le |W_a|\). Multiplicative form: \(P = P_0(1 + W_m \Delta)\) with \(|\Delta| \le 1\), so
\[
\frac{|P - P_0|}{|P_0|} \le |W_m|.
\]
A \(\pm 35\) percent gain error is \(|W_m| = 0.35\), and the plant gain then lies between \(0.65|P_0|\) and \(1.35|P_0|\). Dividing an additive bound by \(|P_0|\) converts it into a relative one at that frequency. The small-gain test on a multiplicative weight will later demand \(|T W_m| < 1\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: Suppose the nominal gain is 7 and a bench measurement reads 9. The absolute error is \(9 - 7 = 2\). The relative error is \(2/7 \approx 0.286\). An additive weight of 2 covers this one measurement with nothing to spare. A multiplicative weight of 0.286 covers it as a fraction of the nominal gain. If the next unit on the production line could be another 10 percent high, the weight has to grow past 0.286. Using 0.286 because it matches today's bench is how an uncertainty model becomes too small.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Relative and absolute errors are not interchangeable: an error of 2 on a gain of 7 is not an error of 2 on a gain of 70. A weight that is larger than the evidence is conservative and can make an otherwise fine spec look impossible. A weight that is smaller than the evidence is optimistic, and the robust test will pass for a set of plants that does not include the real one. Where \(|W_m|\) reaches 1, the model no longer determines the sign of the plant, and the loop gain at that frequency should already be small.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: Robust stability turns \(|W_m|\) into a limit on \(|T|\). Robust performance asks the sensitivity spec to hold for every plant inside the weight, not only for \(P_0\). Both of those tests are only as honest as the weight written down here.
